JUDGMENT

1. Vide this judgment, I propose to dispose of the present appeal filed by the appellants against the impugned order dated 19.12.2018, whereby the Ld. Adjudicating Officer/Additional District Magistrate (East), Delhi, imposed a penalty of Rs.30,000/ under Sections 50 & 51 of the Food Safety & Standards Act, 2006 (in short 'the FSS Act') upon each of the appellants.

2. The facts in brief are that on 09.12.2015 at about 06:30pm, Sh. Bijandera Pal Saroha, Food Safety Officer, took a sample of 'Sugar' for analysis from Sh. Chakresh Aggarwal S/o Sh. Bankey Lal,
FBO/Appellant No. 1  M/s Bharatiya Manav Kalyan Parishad, Harsh Vihar, Delhi110 093.
The said food article was stated to be ready for use.
The FSO tried to associate some public witnesses by requesting customers and passersby but none came forward.

Thereafter, the FSO requested Sh.
Rajpal Singh, the then Field Assistant to join the proceedings as witness, to which he agreed.

The FSO purchased a sample of 'Sugar' for analysis from the FBO/Appellant No. 1 and a credit note dated 09.12.2015 was prepared on the spot for payment of sample price but the sample price was not accepted.
Thereafter, the sample of food article was divided into four equal counterparts and put in four clean and dry bottles.
Each bottle containing the sample was separately packed, fastened and sealed as per the provisions of the FSS Act/Rules & Regulations.
Notice in Form VA was prepared at the spot and copy of the same was given to the FBO/Appellant No. 1.
On 10.12.2015, one counterpart of the aforesaid sample was sent to the Food Analyst.
The other two counterparts were deposited with the Designated Officer Sh. O.P.S. Ahlawat.
As the FBO did not request to send the fourth counterpart of the sample for analysis to NABL accredited laboratory, it was deposited with the Designated Officer.
3. The Food Analyst vide his report No. FSS/1254/2016 dated 14.12.2015 opined that the sample is unsafe because it is not free from insects.

The Food Analyst further opined that the sample is also substandard because moisture exceeds the prescribed maximum limit of 0.5% be weight and Sucrose content is less than the prescribed limit of 98.0% be weight.
4. The FBO was given an opportunity to file an appeal against the report of Food Analyst.
The FBO preferred an appeal and one sample counterpart was sent to the Referral Food Laboratory, Mysore.

The Referral Food Laboratory, Mysore, vide report No. 26F/FSSA/2016 dated 11.04.2016 opined that the sample is "Substandard" as defined under Section 3(1)(zx) of the FSS Act, 2006 as it does not conform to the standards laid down for Plantation White Sugar under the provisions of Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011.

sentences.text: 5. Considering all the facts and circumstances of the case, the Ld. AO/ADM imposed penalty of Rs.30,000/ upon each appellant under Sections 50 & 51 of the FSS Act, 2006.

sentences.text: Sh. Kundan Lal, Ld. Chief PP for the State has submitted that the Ld. AO/ADM has rightly imposed the penalty upon the appellants, as the sample of the food article was found to be substandard.

In support of his arguments, Ld. Chief PP for the State has relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Delhi Administration vs. Vidya Gupta, Crl. Appeal No. 625/2018,
decided on 24.04.2018.

entities.text: Delhi Administration vs. Vidya Gupta, Crl. Appeal No. 625/2018
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 7. Ld. Chief PP for the State has further submitted that in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Delhi Administration vs. Vidya Gupta (Supra), it is clear that the subsequent report of the RFL shall supersede the earlier report of the Public Analyst.
Ld. Chief PP for the State further submitted that in the documents, prepared on the spot at the time of taking the sample, it was specifically mentioned that the sample taken was of 'sugar'.
The technical name of 'plantation sugar' is generally mentioned only at the time of analysis.

It has further been submitted that at that time, the appellants had also not taken any plea that it was 'khandsari sugar'.
8.
Per contra, Sh. R.D. Goel, Ld.
Counsel for the appellants has submitted that the Ld. AO/ADM has passed the order mechanically.

It has been submitted that the Food Analyst as well as the Director,
RFL, have not done characteristic tests to found out whether it was plantation white sugar or it was Khandsari Sugar.
Ld. Counsel further submitted that even in the documents prepared at the time of taking samples, it was not mentioned that it was plantation white sugar.
Ld. Counsel submitted that in fact, it was khandsari sugar.
It has been further submitted that in plantation white sugar, the sucrose content should be 98%, but in the Khandsari Sugar, it was 93.8%.
The report of the Food Analyst and Director, RFL are highly divergent, hence, the sample was not taken in representative manner and the benefit of the doubt should be given to the appellants.

sentences.text: 9. I have heard the submissions of both the parties and perused the record carefully.
10. The Food Analyst as well as Referral Food Laboratory, Mysore have opined that the sample of food article is substandard.

In State of Kerala Vs. Parameswaram Pillai Vasudevan Nair, 1975 Cri LJ 97, it was interalia held as under :
"14.

entities.text: State of Kerala Vs. Parameswaram Pillai Vasudevan Nair, 1975 Cri LJ 97
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Act is a piece of consumer legislation.
It regulates to some extent the consumersupplier relations.
Consumerists demand enforcement of discipline among the producers or manufacturers of food to ensure safety in the realm of food.
The consumer's legitimate ignorance and his almost total dependence on the fairness and competence of those who supply his daily needs have made him a ready target for exploitation.
The Act is intended to protect him against outright frauds.
15. The Act does not make a distinction between cases coming under it on the basis of the degree of adulteration.
It does not provide for aggravation of offence based on the extent of contamination.
The offence and punishment are the same whether the adulteration is great or small.

Food pollution, even if it be only to the slightest extent,
if continued in practice, would adversely affect the health of every man, woman and child in the country.

Hence even marginal or border line variations of the prescribed standards under the Act are matters of serious concern for all and as public interests are involved in them, the maxim, de minimis non curat lex law does not concern itself about trifles, does not apply to them.
16. The standard fixed under the Act is one that is certain.
If it is varied to any extent the certainty of a general standard would be replaced by the vagaries of a fluctuating standard.

The disadvantages of the resulting unpredictability, uncertainty and Sh. Charkesh Aggarwal vs Fso Page 1 Of 15 on 8 November, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/162467825/
4 impossibility of arriving at fair and consistent decisions, are great.

entities.text: Charkesh Aggarwal vs Fso Page 1 Of 15
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 17. The Act does not provide for exemption of marginal or border line variations of the standard from the operation of the Act.
In such circumstances to condone such variations on the ground that they are negligible is virtually to alter the standard itself fixed under the Act.
18. The standards of qualities of the articles have been fixed by the Government under the provisions of the Act after due deliberation and after consulting a committee of competent men.
It is for them to give due allowance for probable errors before fixing a standard.
They may have done it also.
There is no reason to assume otherwise.

Therefore the conclusion is that for an article of food when a standard has been fixed under the Act it has to be observed in every detail."
11.
It is a settled proposition that provisions of such laws are required to be interpreted in strict manner.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Delhi Administration vs. Vidya Gupta (Supra), interalia held as under : "This section must be construed according to the rule of interpretation enunciated in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Kacheroo Mal (1976) 1 SCC 412, which also arose under this Act.

entities.text: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Kacheroo Mal (1976) 1 SCC 412
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
This Court enunciated the Rule as follows:
"5.
The Act has been enacted to curb and remedy the widespread evil of food adulteration, and to ensure the sale of wholesome food to the people.

It is well settled that wherever possible, without unreasonable stretching or straining, the language of such a statute should be construed in a manner which would suppress the mischief, advance the remedy, promote its object, prevent its subtle evasion and foil its artful circumvention......."

12. In respect to the variation of the report of Food Analyst and Director, Referral Food Laboratory,
it was inter alia held as under :
"8. Section 13 lays down the procedure by which the report of the PA that an article of food is adulterated is dealt with.

In brief the procedure is as follows: When a report,
that the article of food is adulterated, is received and a prosecution is instituted, the local health authority is enjoined to forward a copy of the report of such analysis to such person or persons who may have applied for having such food analyzed vide Section 12.

Such persons may, if desired, make an application to the Court to have the sample of the article of food analysed by the Director, and the Court may then dispatch a part of the sample received to the Director.
The Director shall send a certificate specifying the result of the analysis.

Where two parts of the sample have been sent to the Court and one part has been sent by the Court to the Director, the Court is bound to send the remaining part to the local health authority who is bound to destroy it after a certificate is received from the Director vide subsection (2C) of Section 13.

sentences.text: The law accords such great importance to the report from the Director that it prohibits the Court from continuing with the prosecution until the receipt of the certificate from the Director.
Subsection 3 of Section 13 clearly attributes a higher evidentiary value to the certificate from the Director when compared to the report given by the PA.

It reads as follows:
"13. Report of public analyst (1) ..............
(2) ...............
(2A)..............
(2B)..............
(2C)..............
(2D)..............
(2E)..............
(3) The certificate issued by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory [under sub section(2B)]
shall supersede the report given by the public analyst under subsection (1)."
The proviso to subSection 5 provides that the certificate from the Director shall be final and conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein.

The above scheme, particularly sub Section 3 which provides that the certificate of the Director shall supersede the report of the PA and the proviso which makes such a certificate final and conclusive evidence, puts it beyond any shadow of doubt that the report of the PA loses any significance in the proceedings as a piece of evidence.
10. Therefore, there is no reason for the Court to refer to the contents of the report of the PA.
Where there is no reason to refer to its contents of the report of the PA, there is even less reason to refer to the variation between the report of the PA and the Director.
The Court is enjoined by law to consider the contents of the certificate of the Director only.
11. Moreover, this view is no more res integra in view of the judgment of this Court in Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf and another (1999) 2 SCC 400.

entities.text: Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf and another (1999) 2 SCC 400
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This Court held as follows: "Per majority (Thomas and Quadri, JJ.) When Section 13(3) says that the certificate of Director, CFL shall supersede the report, it means
that the report would stand annulled or obliterated.
The word "supersede" in law means "obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void or inefficacious or useless, repeal".

Once the certificate of the Director of the Central Food Laboratory Sh. Charkesh Aggarwal vs Fso Page 1 Of 15 on 8 November, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/162467825/
6 reaches the court, the report of the Public Analyst stands displaced and what may remain is only a fossil of it.
In the above context the proviso to subsection (5) of Section 13 can also be looked at which deals with the evidentiary value of such certificate.
If a fact is declared by a statute as final and conclusive, its impact is crucial because no party can then give evidence for the purpose of disproving that fact.
This is the import of Section 4 of the Evidence Act.
Thus the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of the Central Food Laboratory is threefold.

It annuls or replaces the report of the Public Analyst, it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned."
13.

I consider that in view of the law laid down in Delhi Administration vs. Vidya Gupta (Supra), it is no longer res integra that the report of the Director, RFL, shall prevail and therefore, the variation between the two reports has no significance.

It is also pertinent to mention that even in RFL report,
the sample was found to be substandard.

I do not find any illegality or infirmity in the order of Ld.
AO/ADM.
The appeal is accordingly dismissed.
14. Record of Ld. AO/ADM along with copy of the judgment be sent back, and thereafter appeal file be consigned to Record Room.
